procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated March 29, 1966 of the Madhya Pradesh High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 104 of 1966, which affirmed the trial court's conviction of Munney Khan for murder under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Madhya Pradesh High Court dismissed Munney Khan's appeal summarily, agreeing generally with the conclusions of the trial court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Munney Khan appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's decision.

decision.conviction_status: the conviction under s. 302, l.P.C., is set aside, and the appellant is convicted instead under the first part of section 304, I.P.C.
decision.sentence_status: we set aside the sentence of imprisonment for life and, instead, award him a sentence of seven years' rigorous imprisonment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellant for the offence under s. 302, I.P.C. is justified.

facts: The Court accepted the findings of fact from the lower courts, which were not disputed by the appellant's counsel.
The deceased (Reotisingh) had picked a quarrel with the appellant's brother, overpowered him, and was sitting on his chest, hitting him with his fists.
The appellant, unable to stop the assault with his own fists, stabbed the deceased in the back with a knife.
law: The Court considered the appellant's right of private defense to protect his brother from assault.

When a person exceeds their right of private defense, the resulting offense is culpable homicide not amounting to murder, punishable under the first part of section 304 of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.), rather than murder under section 302, I.P.C.
application: The Court determined that while the appellant had a right to defend his brother, who was being assaulted, he used excessive force by stabbing the deceased with a knife in response to fist blows.
By using a knife, the appellant exceeded his right of private defense.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the conviction for murder under s. 302, I.P.C. was not justified. It held that because the appellant had exceeded his right of private defense, he was guilty of the lesser offense of culpable homicide not amounting to murder. Consequently, the Court set aside the murder conviction and convicted the appellant under the first part of s. 304, I.P.C., reducing his sentence from life imprisonment to seven years' rigorous imprisonment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant had exceeded his right of private defence.

facts: The appellant's brother, Zulfiquar, was being given fist blows by the deceased, Reotisingh.
The court proceeded on the assumption that the deceased was the aggressor, which gave the appellant a right to defend his brother.
In response, the appellant stabbed the deceased in the back with a knife.
The knife blow was aimed at a vital part of the body and was fatal, or at least likely to cause death in the ordinary course of nature.
law: A person has a right of private defence to protect another's body from an offence.
This right is governed by Section 101 of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.).
Section 101 is subject to two key limitations: 1) the person exercising the right cannot cause death, and 2) the force used must not exceed the minimum required for the defence.
If a person causes death while exceeding the right of private defence, the act constitutes culpable homicide not amounting to murder, punishable under s.304, I.P.C.
application: The Court first acknowledged that since the deceased was assaulting the appellant's brother with fists, a right of private defence did accrue to the appellant.
However, the Court found the appellant's response to be disproportionate to the threat. The threat was only "fist blows."
The Court reasoned that responding to fist blows with a knife was, in itself, an excessive use of force and exceeded the right of private defence.
The action became "much more excessive" when the appellant delivered the knife blow to a vital part of the deceased's body (the back), which was likely to be fatal.
The Court concluded that while the appellant was justified in causing some level of hurt to stop the assault, there was no justification for inflicting a fatal blow with a knife.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the appellant had exceeded his right of private defence. Because he used disproportionate force (a fatal knife stab in response to fist blows), his act was not justified. Consequently, he was found guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, punishable under the first part of s.304 of the Indian Penal Code.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant is guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder punishable under the first part of s.304, I.P.C.

facts: The deceased was the aggressor in a quarrel with the appellant's brother.
The deceased overpowered the appellant's brother, threw him to the ground, sat on his chest, and was hitting him with his fists.
The appellant, unable to stop the assault with his own fists, stabbed the deceased in the back with a knife.
law: A person has a right of private defense to protect the body of another person.
This right is subject to limitations: the force used should not exceed what is necessary, and death may not be caused unless there is a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt.
If a person, while exercising the right of private defense, exceeds the power given to them by law and causes death, the offense is not murder but culpable homicide.
An offense of this nature, where there was an intention to cause death or a fatal injury, is punishable under the first part of section 304 of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.).
application: The Court first established that a right of private defense had accrued to the appellant because the deceased was the aggressor and was assaulting his brother.
The Court then reasoned that the appellant's act of stabbing the deceased in the back with a knife would normally constitute murder, as it implies an intention to cause death or a fatal injury.
However, because this act was committed in the exercise of the right of private defense, the case fell under an exception to murder.

The Court found that the appellant had exceeded his right of private defense by using a knife against an unarmed man who was using only his fists. The force used was more than necessary for the purpose of defense.

Since the appellant caused death by exceeding his right of private defense, his crime was determined to be culpable homicide not amounting to murder, falling under the first part of s. 304, I.P.C., due to the intention inferred from the use of the knife.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant had exceeded his right of private defense. Therefore, it set aside his conviction for murder (s. 302, I.P.C.) and found him guilty of the lesser offense of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, punishable under the first part of s. 304, I.P.C.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellant for the offence under s. 302, I.P.C. is justified.
appellant_arguments: The conviction for murder under s. 302, I.P.C. is not justified because the act was committed while exercising the right of private defence to save his brother.
The facts found by the trial court—that the deceased was the aggressor who overpowered the appellant's brother and was beating him—do not support a conviction for murder.
respondent_arguments: The conviction for murder was correctly decided by the Sessions Judge and affirmed by the High Court based on the evidence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant had exceeded his right of private defence.
appellant_arguments: The appellant acted within his right of private defence, as the use of the knife was necessary to rescue his brother who was being overpowered and beaten with fists by the deceased.
respondent_arguments: Even if a right of private defence existed, the appellant exceeded it by using a knife to stab the deceased, which was a disproportionate use of force against someone using only their fists.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant is guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder punishable under the first part of s.304, I.P.C.
appellant_arguments: If the court finds that the right of private defence was exceeded, the offence should be mitigated from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under s. 304, I.P.C.
respondent_arguments: The act constituted murder under s. 302, I.P.C., and the charge should not be reduced, as the excessive force demonstrated an intention to kill.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where death is caused in the exercise of the right of private defense, but by exceeding the power given by that right, the case falls under the exception where culpable homicide does not amount to murder and is punishable under the first part of section 304, I.P.C.
obiter: The right of private defense is essentially a defensive right circumscribed by statute and should not be allowed as a pretext for vindictive, aggressive, or retributive acts.

In a scuffle, it is dangerous as a general rule to grant a right of private defense to either party or their sympathizers; however, if one person is shown to be committing an offense affecting the human body, such a right may arise.
If there is no initial right of private defense, there can be no question of exceeding that right.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Since a right of private defence did exist, the case would fall under the exception under which culpable homicide does not amount to murder on the ground that the death was caused in exercise of right of private defence, but by exceeding that right. An offence of this nature is made punishable under the first part of section 304, l.P.C. Consequently, the conviction of the appellant must be under that provision and not under s. 302. I.P.C.
legal_tests_applied: The right of private defence is governed by s. 101, I.P.C., and is subject to the limitations that in the exercise of the right death may not be caused, and that the force used should not exceed the minimum required to save the person in whose defence it is used.
The right of private defence is codified in ss. 96 to 106 I.P.C. and is available against an act which is an offence.
If there is no initial right of private defence then there can hardly be any question of exceeding that right.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant exceeded his right of private defence because the use of the knife itself was in excess of the right, and it became much more excessive when the blow was given in a vital part of the victim's body and was, in the ordinary course of nature, likely to cause his death.

The appellant's act of giving a blow in the back with a knife leads to an inference that he intended to cause death or at least intended to cause such injury as would, in the ordinary course of nature, result in his death, which would have constituted murder had no right of private defence existed.
why_respondent_won: The court found that the appellant exceeded his right of private defence by using disproportionate force. The use of a knife against an unarmed person was deemed excessive, and even more so when the blow was delivered to a vital part of the body.

While the conviction was reduced from murder, the respondent succeeded in establishing that the appellant's act was not a justifiable exercise of private defence, leading to a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
policy_considerations: The right of private defence is essentially a defensive right circumscribed by the statute, and should not be allowed as a pretext for vindictive, aggressive or retributive purpose.

As this right vests even in strangers for defence of body and property of others against offences, the courts should be careful in seeing that no one on the mere pretext of exercise of right of private defence takes sides in a quarrel between two or more persons and inflicts injuries on one or the other.
When two parties are having a free fight without disclosing their mind it is dangerous as a general rule to clothe either of them or his sympathiser with a right of private defence.
